doc.title: Wayne Bergeron interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 29, 2020

title: First paid gigs: high school top-40 bands
summary: Asked about 'making it', Bergeron recalls playing first trumpet as a freshman and earning $20, then weekend wedding gigs with the band City at 15.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Okay. When I was in music school there was a group of us that were so intent on — we used the term “making it.” We wanted to make it in the music business. And I’m not even sure we knew what it meant but I’m curious if you had that same feeling when you were young, and did you have an idea of what it meant to be successful or to make it?

I did, and on the other side of the coin I really didn’t. But the first time somebody paid me to play the trumpet I got into, when I got into high school I came into the high school jazz band from junior high, and the band director at the high school — and the band director of the junior high school was my first trumpet teacher. He was a very good player and I studied with him through high school. And he told the high school band director, “Hey I’ve got your lead trumpet player coming,” you know, “this kid can play.” And I had a lot of high chops. I’ve had range since I was a little kid, I had kind of natural chops. My range is the same now as it was when I was in the eighth grade, so hopefully I’m a better player but as far as range it’s the same. So I came up into the high school and everybody had to move over. I came in as a ninth grader and the seniors — I played first trumpet as a freshman. And I got into this band, this top 40 band, with some of the seniors from the high school that played weddings and played local gigs. And they played top 40 music of the day. And we played at the Lynwood Bowling Alley I remember, Lynwood Bowl it was called, where I grew up, north of Long Beach. And we played a five hour gig in the lounge, and it was $20. And they handed me a twenty dollar bill at the end of the thing and I went, damn I just made $20 playing the trumpet. You know, a ninth grader making twenty bucks in 1972. It was like twenty bucks. And I go, man, doing what I love the most? So then I got it, we played a few gigs here and there, and then I got into this other band, when I was 15 I remember, because I was a sophomore, I was playing in another community big band and we were talking about how we get work, and the bass trombone player in this band happened to play in another top 40 band from East L.A. called City. And the trumpet player left the band or they fired the trumpet player or something, and I’d been playing in this big band with him. He goes, “Hey man, you want to play in this band, we work almost every weekend. Would you be interested.” And I was like, “Well yeah, of course” you know. And my mom drove me to my first gig because I couldn’t drive. I was 15. And they were all twenties, some of them, they were older than me. The singer was 30 I think at the time.
